```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = nzchar(params$data.file), message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 90)
```

This notebook is a companion of `ms_cacoa.Rmd`: the same cells, counts and annotation on a kNN graph of a Harmony
embedding (`prepare_ms_harmony.R`: 2,000 variable genes, 50 PCs, Harmony by sample, 30 nearest neighbors on 30 Harmony
dimensions, UMAP on the same) instead of the Conos alignment graph. Only the graph-dependent parts are rerun, the
cluster-free density and expression-shift maps; the cell-type-level analyses use the counts and the annotation alone
and are those of the main notebook. The PF companion (`../pf/pf_cacoa_harmony.Rmd`, `../pf/pf_density_diagnosis.md`)
shows why the graph matters there: on the Conos alignment of that cohort the density kernel leaks out of the populations
present in only part of the samples. Here the question is whether the maps of a cohort where the Conos graph worked
change with the alignment.

```{r libs}
library(cacoa)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Load data

```{r load}
seu <- readRDS(params$data.file)
cell.meta <- read.delim(params$meta.file)
sample.meta <- unique(cell.meta[, c("sample", "diagnosis", "stage", "age", "sex", "region", "Capbatch", "Seqbatch", "RIN", "PMI")])
rownames(sample.meta) <- sample.meta$sample
sample.meta <- sample.meta[sort(unique(seu$sample)), -1]
table(sample.meta$diagnosis)
```

```{r construct, message=TRUE}
cao <- Cacoa$new(seu, sample.metadata = sample.meta, sample.per.cell = factor(seu$sample), cell.groups = factor(seu$celltype),
                 embedding = seu@reductions$umap@cell.embeddings, graph.name = "RNA_nn", data.layer = "data", n.cores = params$n.cores)
```

```{r options}
cao$setOptions(n.permutations = 499, seed = 1)
cao$plot.params <- list(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.2, font.size = 3)
cao$sample.groups.palette <- c(Control = "#4575b4", MS = "#d73027")
```

The graph used is Seurat's kNN graph on the Harmony embedding (`RNA_nn`, symmetrized). The thin black lines on the maps
below outline the regions where the cells significant at an adjusted p of 0.05 are the majority (`outline = TRUE`).

```{r embedding, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "cell.groups", title = "cell type"),
                   cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "diagnosis", title = "condition", mark.groups = FALSE, show.legend = TRUE), ncol = 2)
```

```{r set-model}
cao$setModel(~ diagnosis, test = "diagnosis")
```

## Cluster-free density shifts

The same map as in the main notebook: the default diffusion neighborhoods (`scale = "auto"`, a scan over 1, 3 and 5 %
of the cells), each sample's kernel density tested on the log scale with the model, cells adjusted by the pooled
permutation false-discovery rate.

```{r density, fig.width=15, fig.height=4.8, message=TRUE}
cao$estimateCellDensity(method = "graph")
cao$estimateDiffCellDensity()
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotEmbedding(color.by = "cell.groups", title = "cell type"),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(what = "effect", title = "density change (log2 FC)", outline = TRUE),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(title = "adjusted z", outline = TRUE), ncol = 3)
```

On the Harmony graph the scan picks the 1 % scale (neighborhoods of about 470 nuclei), as on the Conos graph, and calls
15,040 of the 46,340 nuclei at FDR 10 % (32 %; 45 % there). The per-type shares below are those at FDR 5 %, as in the
summary plot. The immune expansions are called on both graphs, here more completely (microglia, phagocytes, B and T
cells: 80-100 % of their nuclei, log2 fold changes 1.4-1.8; on Conos 26 % of the T cells and 81-99 % of the others),
and the neuronal depletion is called in the same layers but less completely: 70 % of the EN-L2-3 nuclei (91 % on
Conos), 57 % of EN-L4 (83 %), 48 % of EN-MIX (71 %) and 13 % of EN-L5-6 (53 %; adjusted p 0.12 here, 0.024 there),
although the effects are of similar size (EN-L2-3 -1.1 against -0.9, EN-L5-6 -0.5 against -0.6). Seven types pass the per-type test
(eight on Conos, where EN-L5-6 passes too); the endothelial and stromal nuclei are called at 0 and 25 % here (per type
0.41 and 0.12) and at 20 % and 1 % on the Conos graph (0.072 and 0.076).

The kNN neighborhoods of the graph itself (`scale = NULL`: the stored units of `estimateCellDensity()`, 210 cells
each) are the other neighborhood definition available; they are one hop wide, so they cannot leak the way a kernel can.

```{r density-knn, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.8, message=TRUE}
cao$estimateCellDensity(method = "graph", name = "cell.density.knn")
cao$estimateDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", scale = NULL)
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", what = "effect", title = "kNN units: density change (log2 FC)", outline = TRUE),
                   cao$plotDiffCellDensity(name = "cell.density.knn", title = "kNN units: adjusted z", outline = TRUE), ncol = 2)
```

The kNN neighborhoods (210 nuclei) call the same number of nuclei (15,024) with larger effects (microglia 2.7,
EN-L2-3 -1.9) and the same seven types; IN-PV and EN-L5-6 fall just short (0.051).

## Cluster-free expression shifts

```{r cluster-free-shifts, fig.width=13, fig.height=6, message=TRUE, warning=FALSE}
cao$estimateClusterFreeExpressionShifts(n.permutations = 499)
cao$plotClusterFreeExpressionShifts(adjusted = TRUE, font.size = c(2, 3), outline = TRUE)
```

The expression-shift map is close to the Conos one but somewhat weaker: the scan picks 5 % on both graphs, 74 % of
the nuclei pass FDR 5 % (83 % there) and 14 of 19 types are significant (15). The immune populations
lead here (microglia 1.9, phagocytes 1.7, B and T cells 1.6, then OL, EN-L2-3, IN-VIP and the stromal cells at about 1.5; on Conos the endothelial,
microglial and stromal nuclei at 1.7), EN-L2-3 and EN-L4 are called nearly in full (95-96 % of the nuclei) and EN-MIX
and EN-L5-6 in part (67 % and 43 %; 98-99 % for all four on Conos), the endothelial nuclei drop out (5 % called, 0.12;
96 % and 0.044 there) and
the B cells come in (98 %; 21 % there). IN-PV and IN-SST are not significant on either graph, IN-SV2C only on the Conos
graph (0.046), EN-PYR on neither.

```{r cluster-free-summary, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cell.density")
cao$estimateClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts")
cowplot::plot_grid(cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cell.density"), cao$plotClusterFreeSummary("cluster.free.expr.shifts"), ncol = 2)
```

Per type the maps agree on the main result on both graphs: the immune and microglial expansion with the loss of the
upper-layer excitatory neurons, and the expression shift of the glia. The Conos graph calls the neuronal losses and the
endothelial cells more completely, the Harmony graph the lymphocytes and the stromal cells. On this cohort, where all but the four smallest
populations (B and T cells, phagocytes and stromal cells) are present in most samples of both arms, the alignment
changes the margins, not the picture.
